hints: Start by thinking about natural variation - not all wheat plants in a field are identical, so what kind of plants would be a useful starting point?
If you cannot tell just by looking which plants carry resistance genes, how could you test them using the disease itself?
Once you have identified the survivors that stayed healthy, what is the next logical step to pass on their alleles?
Think about what happens in the next generation - will all the offspring be equally resistant, and what should you do with only the best ones?
Consider why one round of breeding is not enough to get a pure, high-yielding resistant variety - how many cycles are needed?
walkthrough:
Spot the Variation to Start From**
Think of a large field of wheat exposed to a fungal pathogen. Most plants become infected, but a few stay healthy because they happen to carry resistance alleles. Those healthy survivors are your valuable starting material.

Test, Then Breed the Winners**
You deliberately expose plants to the disease so resistance is clearly shown, then you choose only those resistant plants as parents and cross-breed them together. This ensures the resistance alleles are passed into the seeds.

Grow, Re-select and Repeat**
You sow those seeds, grow the offspring, expose them again and keep only the most resistant offspring to breed together. Repeating this selection and interbreeding over many generations concentrates the resistance alleles until you have a stable, disease-resistant variety of wheat.

Final answer: Select wheat plants showing resistance after exposure to disease. Breed selected resistant plants together. Plant seeds and grow offspring. Select resistant offspring and breed together. Repeat for many generations until resistant variety is established, e.g. resistance to rust or mildew.

hints: Think about what happens to the gene pool when you keep breeding only a very small number of chosen parents generation after generation.
Link that narrow gene pool to close inbreeding - what happens when harmful recessive alleles meet, and how does this affect future survival?
walkthrough:
A Smaller Gene Pool Becomes Vulnerable**
When you select only for one trait like disease resistance or yield, you discard many other alleles. The gene pool gets smaller and heterozygosity falls. That means the whole crop is now very similar and can be wiped out together by a new disease or change in climate.

Inbreeding Lets Harmful Alleles Show**
Repeated breeding between closely related, selected plants increases homozygosity. Harmful recessive alleles that were hidden in heterozygotes can now come together in homozygotes and be expressed. This is inbreeding depression, leading to reduced fertility, poorer vigour and accumulation of disadvantageous traits.

Final answer: Reduces genetic variation / increases homozygosity, so population susceptible to environmental change or new disease. Harmful recessive alleles come together and are expressed, causing inbreeding depression / reduced fertility.
